c-structure (Constituent Structure): phrase trees modeling language-specific surface word order
f-structure (Functional Structure): universal Attribute-Value Matrices (AVMs) modeling grammatical relations
Principle of Lexical Integrity: syntactic rules cannot see or alter the internal structure of words
questions.explanation: LFG handles both configurational languages like English and non-configurational languages like Warlpiri equally well, because varying c-structures map onto identical f-structures.

questions.question: What is Government and Binding (GB) Theory, and what is Move-α?
questions.directAnswer: GB Theory is Chomsky's modular principles-and-parameters framework where transformations are generalized into a single operation: Move-α.
questions.vivaAnswer: Formulated by Noam Chomsky in his 1981 book 'Lectures on Government and Binding', GB Theory is a modular, principles-and-parameters generative model. It eliminated complex language-specific transformational rules in favor of a single universal operation: Move-α ('Move any category anywhere, subject to modular constraints'). Derivations proceed through the T-Model: D-Structure maps to S-Structure via Move-α, which then branches to Phonetic Form (PF) for sound and Logical Form (LF) for semantic interpretation.
keyPoints: Noam Chomsky (1981, 'Lectures on Government and Binding')
Move-α: generalized movement rule constrained by modular grammatical principles
T-Model architecture: D-Structure -> S-Structure -> [PF (Sound) / LF (Meaning)]
Universal Grammar consists of invariant Principles and variable Parameters
questions.explanation: GB represented a massive conceptual breakthrough, demonstrating that cross-linguistic syntactic variation could be explained by setting a few universal parameters (e.g. head-directionality).

questions.question: What are the seven core modular subtheories that make up Government and Binding Theory?
questions.directAnswer: X-Bar Theory, Theta Theory, Case Theory, Binding Theory, Bounding Theory, Government Theory, and Control Theory.
questions.vivaAnswer: Government and Binding Theory operates through seven interacting modular subtheories: (1) X-Bar Theory (universal phrase structure schema); (2) Theta (θ) Theory (argument licensing via the Theta Criterion); (3) Case Theory (Case Filter: every overt NP must receive Case); (4) Binding Theory (Principles A, B, and C governing anaphors, pronouns, and R-expressions); (5) Bounding / Subjacency Theory (constraints on movement distance); (6) Government Theory (head c-command and licensing relations); and (7) Control Theory (determining the reference of unpronounced PRO subjects).
keyPoints: 1. X-Bar Theory (phrasal geometry)
2. Theta Theory (argument roles & Theta Criterion)
3. Case Theory (Case Filter)
4. Binding Theory (Principles A, B, C for anaphors/pronouns)
5. Bounding / Subjacency Theory (limits on movement)
6. Government Theory (c-command & proper government)
7. Control Theory (licensing null PRO in non-finite clauses)
questions.explanation: A sentence is grammatical in GB theory if and only if it satisfies the conditions imposed by all seven modular subtheories simultaneously.

questions.question: What are the Theta Criterion and the Case Filter in Government and Binding Theory?
questions.directAnswer: Theta Criterion: each argument gets exactly one theta-role; Case Filter: every overt NP must receive abstract Case.
questions.vivaAnswer: In GB Theory, the Theta Criterion and Case Filter are two universal licensing conditions: The Theta (θ) Criterion dictates that every syntactic argument must be assigned exactly one thematic role (such as Agent or Theme), and each thematic role must be assigned to exactly one argument, preventing missing or extra arguments (*'John put'). The Case Filter dictates that every phonetically overt Noun Phrase must receive abstract Case (Nominative, Accusative, Genitive) from a governing head, or the derivation crashes.
keyPoints: Theta Criterion: 1-to-1 bi-unique mapping between syntactic arguments and semantic theta-roles
Case Filter: *NP if NP has phonetic content and no Case (overt NPs must be Case-marked)
Case drives movement: passive and raising verbs cannot assign Accusative Case, forcing NP movement to Subject position
questions.explanation: The Case Filter explains passivization in GB: because passive participles cannot assign Case to their object, the object must move to the subject position to receive Nominative Case from finite Tense.

questions.question: What is Role and Reference Grammar (RRG) and who formulated it?
questions.directAnswer: RRG is a functional-typological syntactic theory formulated by Robert Van Valin Jr. and William Foley that integrates semantic and discourse functions.
questions.vivaAnswer: Role and Reference Grammar (RRG) is a functional-typological theoretical model founded in the 1980s by Robert D. Van Valin Jr. and William A. Foley. RRG rejects abstract underlying structures, transformational movements, and the autonomy of syntax. Instead, it posits that syntactic structures are directly motivated by semantic representations and discourse-pragmatic communicative functions, designed specifically to capture typologically diverse non-Western and indigenous languages.
keyPoints: Robert D. Van Valin Jr. and William A. Foley (1980s-present)
Functional-typological framework: rejects autonomous generative syntax and movement transformations
Integrates semantic roles, pragmatic focus, and clause structure directly
questions.explanation: RRG is grounded in language typology, providing descriptive elegance for languages that lack rigid configurational structures like English.

questions.question: What is the Layered Structure of the Clause (LSC) and what are semantic Macroroles in Role and Reference Grammar?
questions.directAnswer: LSC organizes clauses into Nucleus (verb), Core (arguments), and Periphery (adjuncts); Macroroles are Actor and Undergoer.
questions.vivaAnswer: In RRG, clause structure is universal and semantically motivated through the Layered Structure of the Clause (LSC), which comprises: (1) The Nucleus, containing the predicate verb; (2) The Core, containing the nucleus and its core arguments; and (3) The Periphery, containing non-arguments and adjunct modifiers. In argument structure, RRG replaces dozens of individual thematic roles with two generalized semantic Macroroles: Actor (the generalized initiator/agent) and Undergoer (the generalized affected participant/patient).
keyPoints: Layered Structure of the Clause (LSC): Nucleus (Predicate) -> Core (Arguments) -> Periphery (Adjuncts)
Pre-Core Slot (PrCS): clause-initial position for fronted wh-words
Semantic Macroroles: Actor (generalized agent/experiencer) and Undergoer (generalized patient/theme)
Parallel Operator Projection: aspect, modality, tense modify specific clause layers
questions.explanation: RRG's layered architecture maps semantic Macroroles directly to syntactic slots without needing abstract transformations or deep structures.

questions.question: How does Relational Grammar model passivization compared to Government and Binding Theory?
questions.directAnswer: RG models passivization as relational promotion (2-to-1) forcing a chômeur; GB models it as NP-movement driven by Case Theory.
questions.vivaAnswer: Relational Grammar and Government and Binding Theory model passivization through completely different theoretical primitives: In RG, passivization is purely relational—the Direct Object (2) is promoted to Subject (1) in the final stratum, which automatically demotes the initial Subject (1) to an ousted 'chômeur' via the Relational Annihilation Law. In GB Theory, passivization is configurational movement (Move-α): the passive verb lacks Accusative Case assignment, forcing the underlying direct object to undergo NP-movement to the empty subject position to satisfy the Case Filter and receive Nominative Case.
keyPoints: Relational Grammar: 2-to-1 promotion; initial 1 becomes Chômeur (purely relational)
GB Theory: NP-movement (Move-α) from object to subject position driven by the Case Filter
RG uses stratal relational diagrams; GB uses configurational hierarchical syntactic trees
questions.explanation: This contrast highlights how different syntactic theories can explain the identical empirical phenomenon (passivization) using either relational terms or structural configurational movement.

questions.question: Provide a master comparative synthesis highlighting the fundamental architectural differences among RG, LFG, GB, and RRG.
questions.directAnswer: GB is derivational with Move-α; LFG is parallel constraint-based; RG is purely relational; and RRG is functional-typological with layered structure.
questions.vivaAnswer: The four theories differ fundamentally in their core primitives and architectures: Government and Binding (GB) is a formal derivational model using abstract movement (Move-α) across structural levels (D-Structure to S-Structure). Lexical-Functional Grammar (LFG) is a non-derivational, parallel constraint-based model linking surface constituent trees (c-structure) with functional matrices (f-structure). Relational Grammar (RG) treats grammatical relations (1, 2, 3) as primitives using stratal networks rather than trees. Role and Reference Grammar (RRG) is a functional-typological, non-derivational framework utilizing the Layered Structure of the Clause (Nucleus, Core, Periphery) and semantic Macroroles.
keyPoints: GB: Derivational (Move-α, T-Model), configurational, universal principles and parameters
LFG: Non-derivational, parallel architectures (c-structure trees + f-structure matrices), lexical integrity
RG: Primitive grammatical relations (1, 2, 3, Chômeurs), multi-stratal derivations without phrase trees
RRG: Functional-typological, non-derivational, Layered Structure of the Clause, Macroroles (Actor/Undergoer)
questions.explanation: This master comparison demonstrates the diversity of 20th-century syntax: moving from Chomsky's formal tree-movement models to non-derivational, relational, and typologically flexible frameworks.
